lesson.title: Silencing 60 Hz Hum: The Precision of a Notch Filter
lesson.summary: A notch filter is a band-reject filter with a very narrow, high-Q stopband tuned to remove one specific troublesome frequency, most famously the 60 Hz or 50 Hz hum picked up from AC power lines, while leaving neighboring frequencies untouched.
lesson.body:
A notch filter is not a different circuit family so much as an extreme case of the Band-Reject Filter you just studied: instead of rejecting a moderately wide band, it targets one specific resonant frequency, the concept from Resonant Frequency, with as narrow and deep a dip as practical. The archetypal use is stripping 60 Hz power-line hum, 50 Hz in much of the world outside North America, out of an audio recording or a biomedical signal like an ECG, without disturbing the frequencies on either side that carry the information you actually want.

A passive notch can be built from the parallel LC tank of Parallel Resonance, placed in series with the signal path so its resonant peak in impedance blocks exactly f0 while letting everything else through at the tank's much lower off-resonance impedance. The resonant frequency is set, as always, by f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), so once you decide the frequency you want to remove, you can solve for the L and C values that put the tank's resonance exactly there.

Suppose you want to notch out 60 Hz hum, and you choose a 10 µF capacitor. Solving f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) for L gives L = 1/((2πf0)²C). First compute (2πf0)² = (2π times 60)², which is (376.99)², about 142,122 in rad per second squared. Then L = 1/(142,122 times 10 times 10 to the minus 6) = 1/1.42122, about 0.704 H, roughly 704 mH. Checking in reverse: LC = 0.704 times 10 times 10 to the minus 6, which is 7.04 times 10 to the minus 6, its square root is 2.653 times 10 to the minus 3, and f0 = 1/(2π times 2.653 times 10 to the minus 3), about 60.0 Hz, confirming the design.

That 704 mH result is worth pausing on: it is a large, bulky, expensive inductor for such a low frequency, and this is exactly why passive LC notch filters become impractical the lower the target frequency gets. In practice, engineers usually build 60 Hz or 50 Hz notch filters as active RC circuits using op-amps, such as the twin-T notch network, which achieve the same sharp rejection using only resistors, capacitors, and gain, with no inductor at all.
